verses.1: Human beings once had no actualized existence.
verses.2: Al-Mizan states that God formed humans from a mixed drop and endowed them with hearing and sight.
verses.3: God showed humans the way, leaving gratitude or ingratitude to them.
verses.4: Chains, collars, and a blaze await the faithless.

verses.22:
Al-Mizan presents Sūrah 76 as a thirty-one-verse Medinan chapter: humanity is created and shown the way, then meets punishment for ingratitude or extensive bliss for righteousness; its final verses order the Prophet to obey God patiently, resist worldly people, and remember and worship Him. It allows that only the first twenty-two verses may be Medinan and the rest Meccan, says Shīʿa reports from the Ahl al-Bayt and mustafīḍah Sunni reports support its Medinan descent, and postpones the wholly Meccan claim to its narration analysis.

Al-Mizan reads the question in (76:1) as an affirmation. Insān is humankind, not Adam, since (76:2) speaks of a mixed drop; ḥīn is an unspecified period and dahr a long span. “Nothing to be mentioned” means not yet an actualized human among named beings, not absolute nonbeing: the material existed before its human actualization. The sequence establishes humanity as originated and therefore created and governed by a Lord, furnished with cognition to find the right path, and destined for torment or lasting bliss according to ingratitude or gratitude.

Al-Mizan takes nuṭfah as semen and amshāj either as its mixed components or the male and female fluids. Ibtilāʾ here is transformation through embryonic stages, not religious testing: the ensuing faʾ in the gift of hearing and sight makes that gift subsequent to transformation, while a proposed taqdīm wa taʾkhīr is unwarranted. Hearing receives the revealed message and sight recognizes divine signs, so their mention shows God’s nurturing direction; repeating insān stresses that He is both Creator and Director. Hidāyah in (76:3) is showing the sabīl, not bringing one to its end. The sabīl is the true religion leading to nearness, and gratitude is sincere servitude; immā describes the guided person, not two alternative paths. People therefore freely become grateful or ungrateful. Their acts remain voluntary although their very willing depends on God’s will, so this dependence does not entail jabr. A translator’s note objects that this distinction alone does not solve free will, says the Qurʾān subjects both wills and acts to God, and refers the fuller answer to divine oneness and the author’s other discussions.

Al-Mizan distinguishes universal intuitive guidance through fiṭrah—an innate direction to true belief and right action—from external verbal guidance through prophets, scriptures, and law. Fiṭrah may be obscured by absorption in apparent causes, vice, obstinacy, or hostility. External guidance reaches humankind collectively but, owing to the limits of transmission, not necessarily each individual; when truth reaches someone God’s proof is complete, while those whom it has not adequately reached are mustaḍʿaf and their case is deferred to God’s forgiveness or punishment. Together these internal and external calls oblige people to follow the religion that accords with fiṭrah, reason, and prophetic teaching.

The chains, collars, and blaze are the ungrateful’s consequence. Al-abrār are not merely beneficent: faith in God, His Messenger, and the Last Day is indispensable, and they do good without seeking gain, patiently preferring God’s will to their own in obedience and against desire. Their camphor drink and spring express their paradisal reward; Al-Mizan further considers it more plausible that these are the embodied reality of their vows and selfless feeding, supported by the present tenses that join their present deeds to their drinking and making the spring flow. Their vows are conventional vows, not merely inner resolutions; the day’s mustaṭīr evil is all-pervading.

In (76:8), the pronoun in “their love for it” most apparently returns to food: they give it despite urgent need. Al-Mizan rejects the alternatives that it means love of God, already stated in (76:9), or love of feeding, which has no praise-worthy force. Asīr retains its ordinary sense of a war captive, not specifically Badr captives, prisoners, slaves, or married women. The verses narrate an actual group of al-abrār and their deeds rather than a hypothetical moral; the captive consequently supports a Medinan sabab al-nuzūl. Their wajh of Allah first means His active attributes and universal mercy: they seek His pleasure alone, abandoning hope of any other recompense. At the essential-attributes level, it means serving the Beautiful One because He is worthy of worship. Jazāʾ here is practical repayment, whereas shukūr is verbal gratitude. Their statement may be spoken to reassure recipients against minnah, or may report the sincere lisān al-ḥāl of their hearts.

Their fear of the “frowning” and qamṭarīr Day means fear of its utmost severity as a day appointed by their Lord for reckoning; hence fear and hope are directed to Him alone. This does not conflict with God’s earlier description of the day’s widespread evil, and preserves every servant’s accountability. God then grants wiqāyah from that harm and receives them with naḍrah, radiant wellbeing, and surūr. Their patience comprises endurance of affliction, obedience, and abstention from sin; because they preferred God’s satisfaction, He replaces their hardships with paradise. There they recline free of heat and bitter cold, are enveloped by shade, and have fruit wholly within reach.

Al-Mizan explains the paradisal service as silver vessels and handleless, spoutless akwāb. “Crystal of silver” may be an analogy for crystal’s silver-like purity or an ellipsis; either the righteous determine the vessels’ exact capacity or the servants do so according to their desire. Ginger is promised because it was a valued drink of the immediate audience, while its paradisal form is superior. Salsabīl may follow an omitted “from” or “I mean,” and al-Rāghib defines it as an accessible, pleasant, fluent, strongly flowing spring. The mukhallad youths retain perpetual freshness; the alternative derivation from an earring is reported, while their pearl likeness may indicate pure complexions, radiant faces, mutual reflected light, or their dispersion through paradise’s gatherings.

Thamma in (76:20) is properly locative, so the first raʾayta means casting one’s gaze there and seeing indescribable bliss and immeasurable dominion. The reported Kufan alternative supplies an omitted mā, unlike the Basran view; the translator notes that either reading yields the same sense and the translation accommodates both. Sundus is fine silk and istabraq thick silk; the righteous also receive silver bracelets. Ṭahūr is a drink that cleanses their inattention to God and the veil of failing to orient toward Him, enabling the praise characteristic of al-mukhlaṣūn. A translator’s note retains the alternative “very pure,” observing that maximal purity can also be purifying. Directly ascribing this drink to the Lord, without intermediary, marks it as superior to the other blessings. Finally, God’s declaration in (76:22) both awards them and performs gratitude for their accepted endeavor. Al-Mizan only tentatively infers female presence among those righteous from the absence of houris; it then attributes to Rūḥ al-maʿānī the specific Ahl al-Bayt account that omits them as courtesy to Fāṭimah al-Batūl.
verses.23: The Qur’an was sent down gradually.
verses.24: Al-Mizan commands patient submission to God and forbids obeying sinners or disbelievers.
verses.25: Al-Mizan directs remembrance morning and evening, with night prostration and glorification.
verses.26: Al-Mizan directs remembrance morning and evening, with night prostration and glorification.
verses.27: They prefer the present life and neglect the grave day ahead.
verses.28: Al-Mizan says God made their joints firm and can replace them with others whenever He wills.
verses.29: The reminder leaves anyone free to take the way to his Lord.
verses.30: Human willing depends on Allah’s will; He is All-Knowing and All-Wise.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan connects (76:23-31) to the reward of the righteous: the Prophet must await God’s command, reject the worldly sinners and disbelievers, and remain in remembrance, prostration, and glorification; (76:29) then generalizes the call to his community. Although this group resembles Meccan discourse, the commentary treats it as compatible with the first twenty-two verses being Medinan and the remainder Meccan.

Al-Mizan stresses that the Qur’an’s gradual descent is exclusively from God—not satanic inspiration or personal desire—through innā, the repeated naḥnu, and tanzīlan confirming nazzalnā. The faʾ in (76:24) draws the consequence: because the Qur’an is from God, its commands are the Prophet’s Lord’s commands and demand patient obedience. A translator’s note preserves an alternative sense of ḥukm as God’s impending judgment, citing similar usage in (10:109), (7:87), (52:48), and (68:48). The prohibitive “or” extends to every habitual sinner and deeply rooted kāfūr, including sinful believers as well as disbelievers. Naming them by these attributes both justifies the prohibition and, in Al-Mizan’s reading, makes it absolute rather than confined to occasions when they invite him to sin or disbelief.

“Remember” means ṣalāh; bukrah and aṣīl mean morning and evening. Prostration in part of the night also means prayer, and the timing may correspond to fajr, ʿaṣr, maghrib, and ʿishāʾ, supporting a Meccan date before the five prescribed prayers; aṣīl may include both ẓuhr and ʿaṣr. A translator’s note records the further possibility that these times signify continual mindfulness rather than specific observances. The night-long glorification is ṣalāt al-layl, either through an implied “during” the long night or through an omitted absolute object meaning a long glorification.

The offenders’ preference for the “immediate” worldly life justifies these orders. Their neglected “weighty” Resurrection Day is grave and inescapable: warāʾahum can mean that it will overtake and encompass them, or that they have cast it behind their backs in disregard. Shadd in (76:28) means God has firmly joined their body—either by sinews, nerves, and muscles or by making its limbs and organs one coordinated whole. The power to replace them with others answers the implied thought that their disbelief defeats God: their creation, life, death, and affairs remain in His hand. It means replacing one generation with another, not, as a less apparent proposal has it, exchanging worldly life for the hereafter.

Al-Mizan identifies “this” reminder with the chapter’s message, as explained under (73:19). The exception in (76:30) qualifies the person’s will rather than directly qualifying action: God’s will first encompasses human willing, so servants freely perform acts attributable to their own volition and no jabr follows; yet they are not independent, since they cannot choose whether their volition itself exists. The shift from third-person audience to “you,” and from the divine “We” to Allah, repudiates imagined independence: as Allah, the origin and end of all, He alone makes willing and effect possible. His knowledge and wisdom introduce (76:31): He wills mercy for believers and the Godwary, while wrongdoers face prepared painful punishment. This present-tense, ongoing divine custom is not arbitrary or ignorant; He treats each group as it deserves and will disclose to all the reality of their deeds.
